---
title: "Pooling experiments: tests, heatmaps, and forking paths"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.5)
```

When several challenge studies exist for one pathogen, it is tempting to
combine them into one dose-response curve: more subjects, narrower intervals,
one number to report. singlehit's pooling functions test whether that is
defensible. This article explains what the tests do, how to read their
results, and how to avoid the main trap, which is letting the test results
choose the groups.

```{r setup}
library(singlehit)
```

## The data

The bundled file holds six human Cryptosporidium challenge experiments
compiled by the [QMRA wiki](https://qmrawiki.org). Every experiment used
healthy adult volunteers, oral exposure, and doses counted in oocysts. Most
differ in the parasite isolate, and one records a different outcome.

```{r data}
path <- system.file("extdata", "cryptosporidium-isolates.csv", package = "singlehit")
raw <- readr::read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = readr::cols(study_id = "c"))
unique(raw[c("study_id", "isolate", "endpoint", "source")])
trials <- split(raw, raw$study_id)
```

Each experiment has four to eight dose groups with a handful of volunteers in
each. That small size matters for everything below.

## What a poolability test asks

`poolability_test()` runs the likelihood-ratio test described by Haas, Rose,
and Gerba. For a set of experiments it:

1. fits each experiment separately and adds up their deviances (the lack of
   fit);
2. stacks every experiment's dose groups and fits one shared curve;
3. takes the difference in deviance as the test statistic. Sharing one curve
   can only fit as well or worse, so the statistic is never negative;
4. compares it with a chi-squared distribution whose degrees of freedom are
   the parameters saved by sharing: one per extra experiment for the
   exponential model (*k*), two per extra experiment for beta-Poisson
   (*alpha* and *N50*).

The p-value answers one narrow question: *if these experiments really shared
one curve, how surprising would this much extra lack of fit be?* A small
p-value is evidence that they do not share a curve. A large one only means the
data could not tell them apart.

## Decide the groups first

The grouping should come from what the experiments are, decided before
looking at any test: same pathogen and isolate, same outcome, same host and
route, same dose unit. For these data the isolate is the obvious candidate,
because isolates of Cryptosporidium are known to differ in infectivity.

singlehit enforces one of these conditions itself. Doses in different units
are not comparable, so datasets that record different `dose_unit` values are
refused:

```{r unit-guard}
relabelled <- trials[c("139", "140")]
relabelled[["140"]]$dose_unit <- "genome copies"
tryCatch(poolability_test(relabelled), error = conditionMessage)
```

Hosts, routes, isolates, and outcomes are not checked. Comparing them is your
job.

## A prespecified test

Messner and colleagues (2001) analysed three isolates challenged in the same
programme: Iowa (139), TAMU (140), and UCP (141). A natural prespecified
question is whether the three isolates share one curve.

```{r confirmatory}
isolates <- poolability_test(trials[c("139", "140", "141")])
isolates[c("model", "lrt_statistic", "df", "p_value", "converged")]
```

```{r confirmatory-values, include = FALSE}
fp <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "p < 0.001" else paste("p =", signif(p, 2))
p_iso_exp <- isolates$p_value[isolates$model == "exponential"]
p_iso_bp <- isolates$p_value[isolates$model == "beta_poisson"]
```

Pooling is rejected under both models (exponential `r fp(p_iso_exp)`,
beta-Poisson `r fp(p_iso_bp)`). The
separate fits show why: the isolates differ several-fold in median
infectious dose.

```{r separate-fits}
n50 <- vapply(c("139", "140", "141"), function(id) {
  fit <- fit_dose_response(trials[[id]], "beta_poisson")
  generics::tidy(fit)$estimate[generics::tidy(fit)$term == "n50"]
}, numeric(1))
round(n50)
```

The defensible conclusion is to model the isolates separately, or to model
the variation between them explicitly (Messner and colleagues used a
hierarchical model for exactly this), rather than to report one pooled curve.
Had the test not rejected pooling, `fit_pooled_dose_response()` would fit the
shared curve to the stacked dose groups.

## Exploring every pair

Sometimes you want to see the structure first: which experiments look
alike? `group_datasets()` tests every pair and then proposes a grouping. The
pairwise p-values are attached to its result.

The two `group_datasets()` searches in this article take about a minute
together, so their results were computed ahead of time by
`data-raw/pooling-article-results.R` and are read from a saved file; everything
else runs as the article is built.

```{r frozen, include = FALSE}
frozen <- readRDS("pooling-results.rds")
if (!isTRUE(all.equal(frozen$data, as.data.frame(raw), check.attributes = FALSE))) {
  stop("The example data changed: rerun data-raw/pooling-article-results.R.")
}
```

```{r explore, eval = FALSE}
# Collect the convergence warnings rather than printing one per refit.
warnings <- character()
explore <- withCallingHandlers(
  group_datasets(trials, method = "agglomerative"),
  warning = function(w) {
    warnings <<- c(warnings, conditionMessage(w))
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
unique(warnings)
pairwise <- attr(explore, "pairwise")
```

```{r explore-frozen, echo = FALSE}
explore <- frozen$explore
warnings <- frozen$warnings
pairwise <- attr(explore, "pairwise")
# A cheap live test of one pair, so a change in the pooling code that moves
# the saved results stops the build instead of passing silently.
live <- suppressWarnings(poolability_test(trials[c("108", "139")]))
live_p <- stats::setNames(live$p_value, live$model)
# The tolerance allows for small optimizer differences between platforms.
if (!isTRUE(all.equal(live_p[["exponential"]], pairwise$exponential["108", "139"], tolerance = 1e-4)) ||
    !isTRUE(all.equal(live_p[["beta_poisson"]], pairwise$beta_poisson["108", "139"], tolerance = 1e-4))) {
  stop("The saved results no longer match the pooling code: rerun data-raw/pooling-article-results.R.")
}
unique(warnings)
```

```{r heatmap, fig.height = 4.8}
cells <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pairwise), function(model) {
  p <- pairwise[[model]]
  grid <- expand.grid(a = rownames(p), b = colnames(p), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  grid$p <- p[cbind(grid$a, grid$b)]
  grid$model <- model
  grid[grid$a != grid$b, ]
}))
cells$model <- factor(cells$model, levels = c("exponential", "beta_poisson"), labels = c("Exponential", "Beta-Poisson"))
cells$b <- factor(cells$b, levels = rev(sort(unique(cells$b))))

ggplot2::ggplot(cells, ggplot2::aes(a, b, fill = p)) +
  ggplot2::geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = ifelse(p < 0.001, "<0.001", signif(p, 2))), size = 3.2) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F4E1D2", high = "#0066A1", limits = c(0, 1), name = "Pairwise p") +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(model)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

```{r explore-values, include = FALSE}
pe <- pairwise$exponential
pb <- pairwise$beta_poisson
others_140 <- setdiff(rownames(pe), "140")
mean_off <- function(p) mean(p[upper.tri(p)])
```

### Reading one cell

Each square is one poolability test of two experiments. **Pale** means a
small p-value: one shared curve fits clearly worse, so there is evidence the
two differ. **Blue** means a large p-value: no evidence of a difference. The
matrix is symmetric, and the diagonal is blank because an experiment always
pools with itself. The grid reports no convergence flags, so read it
alongside the warnings above: any cell can come from a fit that did not
converge.

In the exponential panel:

- **140 (TAMU) is pale against everything** (largest p =
  `r signif(max(pe["140", others_140]), 2)`). TAMU is far more infectious than
  the other isolates, and no shared curve can fit it with any of them.
- **108 and 139 (both Iowa) give p = `r signif(pe["108", "139"], 2)`.** That
  looks like two studies agreeing, but see "Overlapping subjects" below.
- **181 against 139 gives p = `r signif(pe["139", "181"], 2)`.** Experiment
  181 is a different isolate (TU502) *and records a different outcome*
  (diarrhea rather than infection). It should never be pooled with infection
  data, yet the test does not reject it.

### Why the beta-Poisson panel is bluer

The same pairs give larger p-values under beta-Poisson (mean
`r signif(mean_off(pb), 2)` against `r signif(mean_off(pe), 2)` for
exponential). The experiments did not become more alike; the test became
weaker. The second parameter lets each curve bend to fit its own data, the
test has two degrees of freedom instead of one (a higher bar to reject), and
with four to eight doses per experiment the approximate beta-Poisson model is
poorly determined. Beta-Poisson comparisons of small studies typically have
little power.

## Three mistakes to avoid

**"Not rejected" is not "the same".** A p-value of
`r signif(pe["139", "181"], 2)` does not show that experiments 139 and 181
share a curve; it shows these data cannot tell them apart. With so few
volunteers, very different experiments often pass.

**Pairwise results do not chain.** "A pools with B" and "B pools with C" does
not mean A, B, and C share one curve. A group needs one curve for all its
members, which is a stricter test than any pair.

**Many tests, no correction.** Each panel holds `r choose(nrow(pe), 2)`
tests, `r 2 * choose(nrow(pe), 2)` in all. At alpha = 0.05 you would expect
a "rejection" or two by chance even if every experiment were identical, and
pairs can pass just as arbitrarily. None of these p-values are adjusted.

## Groupings are not unique

`group_datasets()` turns the pairwise results into groups. The agglomerative
method (above) repeatedly merges the most compatible pair of groups, testing
each merged group as a whole, until no merge passes; the exhaustive
method searches every way of splitting the experiments (203 ways for six) for
the fewest groups that all pass.

```{r exhaustive-code, eval = FALSE}
exhaustive <- suppressWarnings(group_datasets(trials, method = "exhaustive"))
```

```{r exhaustive-frozen, include = FALSE}
exhaustive <- frozen$exhaustive
```

```{r exhaustive}
groups <- function(result, model) {
  rows <- result[result$model == model, ]
  vapply(split(rows$dataset, rows$group), paste, character(1), collapse = " + ")
}
list(
  agglomerative = list(exponential = groups(explore, "exponential"), beta_poisson = groups(explore, "beta_poisson")),
  exhaustive = list(exponential = groups(exhaustive, "exponential"), beta_poisson = groups(exhaustive, "beta_poisson"))
)
```

```{r groups-values, include = FALSE}
together <- function(result, model, a, b) {
  rows <- result[result$model == model, ]
  rows$group[rows$dataset == a] == rows$group[rows$dataset == b]
}
```

The same data give different groupings depending on the model and the
search method. Under beta-Poisson, the exhaustive search
`r if (together(exhaustive, "beta_poisson", "108", "139")) "keeps" else "separates"`
the two Iowa experiments, even though the heatmap shows no difference
between them (p = `r signif(pb["108", "139"], 2)`). Several groupings pass the tests, and the search reports one of
them. In both methods the TU502 diarrhea experiment (181) joins an infection
group.

This is the forking-paths problem
([issue #20](https://github.com/seanthimons/singlehit/issues/20)): when the data choose the
groups, a pooled curve fitted to a chosen group, and its test, are biased
toward pooling. Use the exploration to sanity-check a grouping you decided
on, not to choose one.

## Overlapping subjects

Look at experiments 108 and 139 side by side:

```{r overlap}
overlap <- merge(
  trials[["108"]][c("dose", "positive", "negative")],
  trials[["139"]][c("dose", "positive", "negative")],
  by = "dose", suffixes = c("_108", "_139")
)
overlap
```

```{r overlap-values, include = FALSE}
same_rows <- sum(overlap$positive_108 == overlap$positive_139 & overlap$negative_108 == overlap$negative_139)
```

The counts are identical at `r same_rows` of `r nrow(overlap)` doses and
differ by one volunteer at the others. That strongly suggests both entries
report largely the same Iowa volunteers: DuPont and colleagues (1995)
reported an Iowa-isolate challenge, and Messner and colleagues (2001)
analysed Iowa-isolate data from the same investigators (Chappell and
Okhuysen are authors of both). The poolability test
assumes independent samples, so its p-value of
`r signif(pe["108", "139"], 2)` says nothing here, and pooling the two would
count the same people twice. Check where each experiment's subjects came
from before pooling.

## Reporting

A paragraph that reports this honestly might read:

> Pairwise likelihood-ratio tests (exponential model,
> `r choose(nrow(pe), 2)` unadjusted comparisons) showed that the TAMU
> isolate differed from every other experiment (p < 0.01), and a test of the
> three isolates studied by Messner et al. (2001) rejected a common curve
> (p < 0.001). We therefore modelled isolates separately. Beta-Poisson
> comparisons had low power (two degrees of freedom, four to eight doses per
> study) and some fits did not converge, so we did not use them to group
> experiments. Experiments 108 and 139 appear to share subjects and were not
> pooled.

## In the Shiny app

The app's Pooling tab runs the same functions. It requires a written reason
before each test, keeps a session log of every test and exploration, and
marks any set chosen from an exploration, or lying within one, as
*data-informed* in the tab, the log, and the label of pooled data sent to
Fit. Its Library tab can filter experiments by strain or isolate, so a
grouping can be decided before anything is tested.

```{r premises, include = FALSE}
# The text above interprets these results; stop the build if they change.
stopifnot(
  p_iso_exp < 0.001,
  p_iso_bp < 0.05,
  all(pe["140", others_140] < 0.01),
  pe["108", "139"] > 0.05,
  pe["139", "181"] > 0.05,
  mean_off(pb) > mean_off(pe),
  !identical(groups(explore, "beta_poisson"), groups(exhaustive, "beta_poisson")),
  !together(exhaustive, "beta_poisson", "108", "139"),
  # 181 (diarrhea) shares a group with an infection experiment in every result.
  all(vapply(list(explore, exhaustive), function(result) {
    all(vapply(c("exponential", "beta_poisson"), function(model) {
      any(vapply(c("108", "139", "140", "141", "183"), function(id) together(result, model, id, "181"), logical(1)))
    }, logical(1)))
  }, logical(1))),
  same_rows >= 6,
  pb["108", "139"] > 0.05,
  length(warnings) > 0,
  max(n50) / min(n50) > 3
)
```
